analysis.one_liner: A large package of permanent business tax cuts and sweeping limits on federal regulation, financial oversight, and the health care employer mandate.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 253-163 on September 18, 2014, but the Senate never voted, and it died on the Senate calendar when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a giant catch-all bill. Division I made several business tax breaks permanent — the research credit, $500,000 equipment expensing, S corporation rules, and 50% 'bonus depreciation' — and explicitly waived the usual pay-as-you-go rule, so none of the lost revenue had to be offset. It also changed the Affordable Care Act so employees working under 40 hours no longer count toward the employer coverage mandate and let employers exclude employees covered by veterans' or military health programs. The rest of the bill rewired how Washington regulates: every 'major' federal rule would need an affirmative vote of Congress to take effect, new procedural hurdles and court review would slow or kill rules, private equity fund advisers would be exempt from SEC registration, a 2.3% excise tax on medical devices would be repealed, mining permits would face faster approval with less environmental review, and national forests would be managed to guarantee timber sales. The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote; the Senate placed it on its calendar and never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries were businesses and specific industries. Corporations would have gained permanent tax breaks without any offsetting revenue. Private equity fund advisers would have escaped SEC registration and reporting. Medical device makers would have shed a 2.3% excise tax. Large employers would have faced a weaker Affordable Care Act mandate. Timber and mining companies would have gained easier access to federal land with lighter environmental review and fewer citizen lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Businesses, private equity, device makers, timber and mining firms

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the research tax credit (at a new 20% rate), the $500,000 small-business expensing allowance, several S corporation tax rules, and the 50% 'bonus depreciation' write-off for new equipment.
Waives statutory pay-as-you-go (PAYGO) scorecards for every tax title, meaning the bill's lost revenue did not have to be paid for with offsets.
Repeals the 2.3% excise tax on medical devices, a revenue source for the Affordable Care Act.
Exempts private equity fund investment advisers from registration and reporting under the Investment Advisers Act, as long as each fund's borrowing does not exceed twice its invested capital.
Exempts certain merger-and-acquisition brokers from Securities Exchange Act registration, for deals involving private companies with under $25 million in earnings or $250 million in revenue.

Requires an affirmative joint resolution of Congress before any 'major' federal rule (annual economic effect of $50 million or more, any EPA rule significantly affecting farms, any rule implementing a carbon tax, or any Affordable Care Act rule) can take effect; if Congress does not act within 70 days, the rule dies.

Rewrites rulemaking procedure so agencies must hold hearings for high-impact rules, use a stricter evidence standard, choose the least-costly option, and allows courts to refuse to defer to agency judgments.
Requires every rule's supporting information to be posted online for six months before it can take effect.

Lets a mining agency approve a permit without treating it as major federal action under the National Environmental Policy Act if existing procedures are deemed adequate, and bars courts from awarding attorney fees to challengers of mining permits and limits suits to a 60-day window.

Directs the Forest Service to set up 'Forest Reserve Revenue Areas' in every national forest unit managed to hit a required timber volume, and moves Oregon's O&C lands into a trust managed like private forest land to produce maximum sustained timber revenue.
Permanently extends the ban on state and local taxes on Internet access and on multiple or discriminatory taxes on electronic commerce.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, ordinary taxpayers would have borne the cost of the unpaid-for tax breaks through larger deficits. Workers could have lost employer health coverage: raising the full-time threshold from 30 to 40 hours lets employers schedule people at 39 hours to avoid the mandate. Communities that rely on federal health, safety, and environmental rules would have faced a rulemaking system designed so major rules rarely survive, plus expanded logging and mining on public lands with limited environmental review and reduced ability to sue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, workers at risk of losing coverage, and rule-protected communities

drawbacks.text: Redefining full-time work as 40 hours a week for the employer mandate gives employers a clear incentive to cut employees' hours below 40 so they no longer count, moving those workers off employer coverage.
The permanent tax cuts are not offset: the bill directs that their budgetary effects not be entered on any PAYGO scorecard, so the revenue loss adds to the deficit.

The requirement that Congress affirmatively approve every major rule within 70 days, or the rule dies, would let a single chamber's inaction block major public health, safety, and environmental protections, including any rule implementing a carbon tax.
Exempting private equity advisers from Investment Advisers Act registration removes the Dodd-Frank-era SEC oversight of a sector managing large pools of institutional and pension money.
The mining title weakens environmental review of mine permits, limits who can sue and when, and bars fee awards to prevailing challengers, tilting the process toward permit holders.

The forest title requires timber production targets in designated national forest areas and manages Oregon's O&C lands like private forests, prioritizing timber revenue over the multiple-use management that governs federal lands.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A few pieces are defensible on their own, like making the stopgap research credit and small-business expensing rules permanent and keeping Internet access tax-free. But the package as a whole asks ordinary people to fund permanent business tax cuts they did not have to offset, accept a weaker employer health mandate that shifts costs onto hourly workers, and live under a regulatory system rebuilt so that most major protections would need a vote of a divided Congress to exist. The regulatory titles go well beyond transparency into substantive paralysis, and the public-lands titles trade environmental review for industry access.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 253-163 on September 18, 2014, arrived in the Senate in November, and was placed on the Senate calendar — but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Dave Camp (R-MI), chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, introduced the bill on September 15, 2014; it was referred to nine House committees.

The Rules Committee cleared the way with H. Res. 727, which allowed two hours of debate, waived points of order against the bill's provisions, and permitted only one motion to recommit — so no amendments were allowed on the floor.

On September 18, 2014, Representative Tim Bishop (D-NY) offered a motion to recommit with instructions that would have added a tax credit for bringing jobs back from overseas, denied deductions for offshoring costs, made corporate inversions harder, denied the bill's tax benefits to inverted corporations, and forced votes on minimum wage, pay equity, student loan refinancing, paid sick leave, and child care bills. It failed 191-218, with 191 of 199 Democrats in favor and every voting Republican opposed.
The House passed the bill 253-163: 221 of 232 Republicans voted yes (1 no), as did 32 of 199 Democrats (162 no).
The Senate received the bill on November 12, 2014, and placed it on its legislative calendar under General Orders on November 13, but never took a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, none of its tax cuts, mandate changes, or regulatory rollbacks took effect. Workers whose employer coverage depends on the 30-hour rule and communities that rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and financial oversight are better off; the industries that stood to gain — medical device makers, private equity, timber and mining companies, and corporations claiming the tax breaks — got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers and rule-dependent communities; industries got nothing

for.name: Rep. Dave Camp
for.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 15, 2014, and steered its tax titles through the House.

for.name: 221 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage; only one Republican voted no.

for.name: 32 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, providing the margin that got the bill to 253 votes.

against.name: 162 of 199 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage; 191 of 199 also voted for the Bishop motion to recommit that would have added anti-offshoring tax rules and forced votes on wage and benefit bills.

against.name: Rep. Tim Bishop
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add anti-offshoring and anti-inversion tax provisions and require votes on the Fair Minimum Wage Act, Paycheck Fairness Act, student loan refinancing, the Healthy Families Act, and the Strong Start for America's Children Act; the motion failed 191-218.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar in November 2014.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: The administration publicly warned it would veto the health-care and regulatory components of the House package, including the 40-hour redefinition of full-time work.

sides.party_line_note: The final vote split sharply by party: 221 of 232 Republicans voted yes against just 32 of 199 Democrats, and the motion to recommit failed 191-218 with 191 Democrats in favor and zero Republicans.

industries.industry: Corporations claiming tax breaks (research-intensive firms, equipment buyers, S corporations)
industries.note: The bill makes several business tax breaks permanent and waives PAYGO, so the lost revenue is not offset — the public pays for it through larger deficits while the benefits concentrate among businesses wealthy enough to use the provisions.

Exempt from Investment Advisers Act registration and reporting as long as fund borrowing stays under twice invested capital, undoing Dodd-Frank oversight of advisers managing pension and institutional money.
The bill repeals the 2.3% excise tax on their sales, a dedicated revenue stream for the Affordable Care Act's coverage expansion; the industry sheds a cost while the funding it supplied disappears.

The bill mandates timber-production areas in every national forest unit and manages Oregon's O&C lands like private forests for maximum sustained revenue, guaranteeing the industry wood supply at the expense of multiple-use management.

Expedited permitting for strategic and critical minerals, agency authority to bypass treating permits as major NEPA actions, a 60-day limit on lawsuits, and a ban on attorney fee awards tilt federal mine permitting toward operators.

industries.industry: Large employers facing the Affordable Care Act mandate
industries.note: Raising the full-time threshold from 30 to 40 hours and excluding employees on TRICARE or VA coverage shrinks the pool of workers that trigger the mandate; the corresponding risk is that workers get their hours cut below 40 and lose the coverage the rule was meant to protect.

The bill permanently extends the moratorium on state and local taxes on Internet access and on multiple or discriminatory taxes on e-commerce, a benefit that runs with consumers' interest in cheaper access.
